findings.title: Wikipedia covers every site.
findings.body: Every proposed site has an English Wikipedia article (or a section of one), and the Central Park article alone is about 280 KB. Seneca Village (66 KB) and the Ramble and Lake (58 KB) are especially strong.

findings.title: The park's own voices need a deal.
findings.body: The Central Park Conservancy publishes no reuse terms and NYC Parks falls under nyc.gov's "All rights are reserved". Their site texts, historical signs and tours are outreach, and the Conservancy is the natural partner, as the Frick was.

findings.title: Founding documents are public domain.
findings.body: The Board of Commissioners' annual reports (1858 onward, with Olmsted and Vaux's reports), Clarence Cook's 1869 description of the park and Peet's 1903 Trees and Shrubs of Central Park are on Internet Archive. They are period sources and get historical framing.

findings.title: Location is the open design question.
findings.body: Indoor venues get the room from the QR code or link a visitor opens. In a park, visitors wander. The app already sends the visitor's GPS position to the guide, but the guide doesn't use it yet. Deferred: site coordinates are recorded now for whichever approach is chosen.

findings.title: Two topics need care.
findings.body: Seneca Village: the displacement of a Black landowning community in 1857, stated plainly. Strawberry Fields: John Lennon's murder is covered factually, and song lyrics are never quoted.

exhibitions.name: Seneca Village
exhibitions.notes: A largely Black community of landowners, with churches and a school, displaced by eminent domain in 1857 to build the park. Stated plainly, from sources.

exhibitions.name: The Arsenal
exhibitions.notes: Built 1847–51, before the park; NYC Parks headquarters. Next to the zoo, which is a separate venue.

exhibitions.name: Cleopatra's Needle
exhibitions.notes: Ancient Egyptian obelisk of Thutmose III, erected behind the Met in 1881.

exhibitions.name: Strawberry Fields
exhibitions.notes: Memorial to John Lennon with the Imagine mosaic. Song lyrics are never quoted. The murder of John Lennon at the Dakota is covered factually.

exhibitions.name: The Mall and Literary Walk
exhibitions.notes: Elm-lined promenade; statues of Shakespeare, Burns, Scott, Halleck and Columbus on the Literary Walk.

exhibitions.name: Alice in Wonderland
exhibitions.notes: José de Creeft's bronze (1959) at Conservatory Water.

exhibitions.name: Hans Christian Andersen
exhibitions.notes: Georg Lober's bronze (1956); summer storytelling.

exhibitions.name: Balto
exhibitions.notes: Frederick Roth's statue (1925) of the sled dog from the 1925 serum run to Nome.

exhibitions.name: Bethesda Terrace and Fountain
exhibitions.notes: The park's formal centre; Emma Stebbins's Angel of the Waters (1873), the first public art commission for a woman in New York City.

exhibitions.name: Bow Bridge
exhibitions.notes: Cast-iron bridge over the Lake (1862), Vaux and Mould. HABS documented it.

exhibitions.name: Belvedere Castle
exhibitions.notes: Vaux and Mould's folly (1869) on Vista Rock; weather station.

exhibitions.name: The Dairy
exhibitions.notes: Victorian Gothic building (1870), now a visitor centre.

exhibitions.name: The Pond, Hallett Nature Sanctuary and Gapstow Bridge
exhibitions.notes: South-east corner: the Pond, Gapstow Bridge and the Hallett Nature Sanctuary.

exhibitions.name: The Ramble and the Lake
exhibitions.notes: Wooded paths around the Lake; one of the country's best spring migration spots for birds.

exhibitions.name: The Great Lawn and Turtle Pond
exhibitions.notes: Former receiving reservoir (drained 1930s); concerts and ballfields.

exhibitions.name: Sheep Meadow
exhibitions.notes: Grazed by sheep until 1934; a quiet lawn.

exhibitions.name: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir
exhibitions.notes: Croton water system reservoir (1862); running track; waterbirds.

exhibitions.name: North Woods, the Ravine and North Meadow
exhibitions.notes: The park's wildest landscape: the Loch, the Ravine, Huddlestone Arch.

exhibitions.name: Harlem Meer
exhibitions.notes: Lake at the north-east corner; Dana Discovery Center.

exhibitions.name: Conservatory Garden
exhibitions.notes: Formal garden in Italian, French and English styles; Vanderbilt Gate.

exhibitions.name: Shakespeare Garden
exhibitions.notes: Garden of plants named in Shakespeare's works, below Belvedere Castle.

exhibitions.name: Conservatory Water
exhibitions.notes: Model boat pond; Alice and Andersen statues nearby.

exhibitions.name: The Carousel
exhibitions.notes: Friedrich Carousel (1908), moved here in 1951.

exhibitions.name: Wollman Rink
exhibitions.notes: Skating rink (1949).

exhibitions.name: Delacorte Theater
exhibitions.notes: Open-air theater (1962); Shakespeare in the Park.

decisions.decision: Central Park is the venue (one Strapi Place); its 25 sites are Dropbox-defined exhibitions, as at the Frick.
Out of scope here; a separate venue later (Wildlife Conservation Society).
Deferred: QR codes, GPS geofences or both is a larger question to resolve. Site coordinates are recorded now so either approach can use them.

Pulled and staged: places/_central-park (429 files: 25 sites with their Wikipedia article, prompt.md and card.txt, 21 site images, 35 monuments and features from Wikidata with 34 images, 9 public-domain books, venue history) and _library (5 new topics, 17 new artist folders for the park's sculptors). About 2,000 chunks; all pass the ingest's rules.

Monuments go to the nearest site within 250 m (Wikidata coordinates), with 14 corrections by hand (Literary Walk statues to the Mall, King Jagiello to the Great Lawn, Ramble Arch to the Ramble, edge-of-park statues to the park level). placements.json records the evidence for each.

Cards may use public domain, CC0, CC BY or CC BY-SA photos; each card carries its photo credit and source link (card-credit.txt), shown under the image on the landing page. 21 of 25 sites have a card; the 4 without have no Wikidata item or photo (Bow Bridge, the Dairy, the Reservoir, Shakespeare Garden).
Seneca Village's displacement is stated plainly from sources (as with Frick's labor history). Song lyrics are never ingested or quoted; John Lennon's murder is covered factually.
